1. Station Utilization & Demand Analysis

The network comprises 40 stations evenly split between Urban and Highway locations. Average charging demand is tightly distributed (51.1–56.1), indicating a relatively balanced load across the fleet, but top performers such as ST012 (56.1) and ST003 (55.1) still outrank laggards like ST011 (51.1) by roughly 10%.

Station load during Peak hours surges to 84.1 kW on average—more than double the Off-Peak baseline of 34.7 kW. This 2.4× swing signals significant grid stress concentration in a narrow temporal window.

2. Queue Length & Waiting Time Analysis

Contrary to intuition, Off-Peak periods show slightly higher waiting times (9.58 min) and queue lengths (4.65 vehicles) than Peak periods (9.43 min, 4.50 vehicles). This suggests the scheduling or demand-prediction algorithm may be over-allocating capacity to Peak windows while under-serving Off-Peak arrivals, or that Off-Peak staffing and charger availability is insufficient.

Highway stations experience marginally longer queues in Off-Peak hours (4.70 vs 4.60 Urban), while Peak queues are nearly identical across location types. Vehicle type has minimal impact on wait times (Bus 9.61 min, Car 9.54 min, Two-Wheeler 9.43 min), indicating the queue discipline is largely first-come-first-served rather than priority-weighted.

3. Energy Consumption & Grid Load Patterns

Peak-hour station load averages 84.1 kW versus 34.7 kW Off-Peak—a 142% increase that far outpaces the modest change in per-session energy consumption (39.1 kWh overall, nearly flat across time slots). This divergence implies that Peak stress is driven by simultaneity (many vehicles charging concurrently) rather than by individual session intensity.

Hourly load profiling reveals the highest grid stress occurs at 17:00–19:00 (≈84.7–85.0 kW), aligning with typical evening commute peaks. Morning peaks around 08:00–10:00 are only marginally lower (≈83.9–84.0 kW). The grid therefore faces a sustained high-load window spanning roughly 08:00–20:00.

4. Renewable Energy Integration & Dynamic Pricing

The overall renewable energy ratio stands at 35.4%, with minimal variation between Urban (35.7%) and Highway (35.2%) locations. However, the ratio collapses during Peak hours to 28.9–29.4% while rising to 39.1–39.4% Off-Peak. This 10-percentage-point swing indicates that renewable supply is not scaling with demand; the grid likely falls back on fossil baseload during high-load periods.

Weather conditions show surprisingly little effect: Clear skies yield 35.7% renewables versus 35.1% Cloudy and 35.4% Rainy. Dynamic pricing also exhibits weak differentiation—Peak prices (9.94) are only marginally below Off-Peak (9.97), and the correlation between price and demand is negligible (−0.012). The current pricing signal is too flat to incentivize demand shifting.

5. Vehicle Charging Behavior & Session Profiles

The fleet is evenly distributed across vehicle types (~33% each), with nearly identical charging durations (≈179 min) and only modest differences in energy consumed per session (Bus 39.4 kWh, Car 39.1 kWh, Two-Wheeler 38.7 kWh). Battery capacities are also tightly clustered around 61 kWh, suggesting the dataset models a relatively homogeneous fleet rather than a diverse real-world mix.

Charging priority is well-balanced across Low (33.3%), Medium (34.9%), and High (31.8%) tiers, with no vehicle type dominating any priority band. This equitable distribution supports a fair-access policy but may miss opportunities to fast-track high-value or low-SOC vehicles.

6. Optimization Insights & Recommendations

The optimization reward metric is strongly correlated with renewable availability (r = +0.59) and inversely correlated with station load (r = −0.58). Peak rewards are deeply negative (−19.8) compared to Off-Peak (−7.1), confirming that current operations are systematically suboptimal during high-demand windows. The following actions are recommended:

1. Implement Time-of-Use Pricing with Stronger Differentials

Current Peak/Off-Peak price spreads are negligible (~0.03 units). Increase Off-Peak discounts and introduce Mid-Peak tiers to flatten the demand curve. Target a 15–20% price reduction during 00:00–06:00 and a 10–15% surcharge during 17:00–20:00 to shift 10–15% of load out of the evening peak.

2. Deploy Predictive Queue Management

Off-Peak queues are unexpectedly long, suggesting under-provisioned staffing or poor arrival forecasting. Deploy ML-based demand prediction (using traffic density, weather, and historical patterns) to pre-activate standby chargers 30–60 minutes before predicted surges.

3. Augment Renewable Buffer Storage for Peak Hours

Renewable penetration drops 10 points during Peak. Install battery energy storage systems (BESS) charged during high-renewable Off-Peak hours and discharged during Peak to maintain >35% renewable ratio across all time slots, directly improving optimization reward.

4. Introduce Dynamic Priority Weighting

Because all vehicle types exhibit similar wait times, the priority system is effectively neutral. Consider weighting priority by SOC deficit (lower initial SOC = higher priority) and by vehicle class (buses serving public transit receive elevated priority) to reduce system-wide energy throughput time.

5. Load-Balance Across the Top 5 and Bottom 5 Stations

ST012 and ST003 run 10% above ST011 in demand. Use digital signage, in-app routing, and small price nudges (e.g., −2% at underutilized stations) to steer 5–8% of demand from top-tier to bottom-tier stations, improving network-wide utilization parity.

6. Expand Charger Count at High-Load Evening Corridors

With sustained 84 kW loads from 08:00–20:00, the current 40-station fleet is capacity-constrained for more than half the day. Prioritize capex for additional fast chargers (≥150 kW) at Urban stations experiencing the highest evening peaks, where land and grid access are more feasible than Highway expansions.
